endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Users must understand that if certain information is not recorded in the clinical record, the AI will not be able to retrieve it.

endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)

evidence.title: Evaluating Clinical Symptom Extraction and Reasoning in Local Large Language Models: A Proof-of-Concept Study of Symptom-Specific Performance in Cardiology
evidence.effect: Both models inferred symptoms from ECG findings, tachycardia, or heart-failure diagnosis despite no explicit symptom documentation.
evidence.quote: Review of the reasoning outputs showed that, in some cases, both models inferred palpitations from electrocardiographic findings or documented tachycardia, and fatigability from the underlying diagnosis of heart failure, despite the absence of explicit symptom documentation.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether labeling model assumptions or flagging missing chart data changes how clinicians interpret generative AI output. One simulated study from Japan found that two models inferred undocumented symptoms from ECG findings, tachycardia, or a heart-failure diagnosis, which suggests the hazard exists.

perspectives.view: No study evaluates the practice, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single hazard study is descriptive, offline, and small (80 symptom-case labels from 10 cases). It shows that models inferred symptoms absent from the record. It does not show that visual labeling or missing-data flags would reduce clinician misreading.

In the Japanese study, both models attributed symptoms to patients based on ECG findings, tachycardia, or a heart-failure diagnosis without explicit documentation. If clinicians accept such inferences as charted facts, errors could propagate into diagnosis or treatment. Whether distinguishing inferred from verified content would catch these errors before they reach patients remains untested.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide states as a must that users understand the AI cannot retrieve information absent from the record, and a commentary on portal message guardrails recommends surfacing uncertainty and missing-context prompts. These endorsements rest on expert consensus rather than tested outcomes, and neither specifies how the distinction should be displayed.

The hazard study used Japanese-language clinical records, so it offers some signal outside English documentation. It did not examine Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy settings, where records may be more fragmented and the gap between documented and inferred information could be larger.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare clinician interpretation, error rates, and downstream decisions when generative AI output does or does not mark inferred content and missing chart data, using live EHR workflows and measuring alert burden and whether clinicians notice the labels.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists in any population. The one hazard study used non-English (Japanese) records in a simulated setting and did not include Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency patients in U.S. care, or low-literacy populations, so effects in those settings are unknown.
